pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** What Is an Earthquake

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** Not a KS1 science topic; England places earthquakes in the **KS2 Geography** programme of study ('volcanoes and earthquakes', ages 7–11). At 5–7 teach as enrichment supported by KS1 'Working scientifically' (observing, describing, using simple sources).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No K–2 PE names earthquakes directly; the anchor is **2-ESS1-1** ('… Earth events can occur quickly or slowly'), whose clarification names 'earthquakes, which happen quickly' — an earthquake is a canonical fast Earth event. CCC [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1, 2-ESS2-1].'

- **Operational details:** At 5–7 an earthquake is 'a sudden shaking of the ground'. Two ideas to secure: (1) it is the GROUND ITSELF that shakes (not just objects, not an explosion), and (2) earthquakes vary in strength — from so weak you barely notice, to strong enough to knock things over. Because a real earthquake can't be shown live, the felt experience is best simulated: shake a scene and let children see cups rattle, pictures tilt, shelves wobble. Connect to body experience ('imagine the whole floor wobbling like jelly'). Keep the CAUSE (rocks breaking/moving underground, releasing energy) for the 7–9 'Why Earthquakes Happen' topic; here, describe WHAT it is and what it feels like. Address the Hollywood image early: the ground shakes, it does not usually 'open up and swallow' people.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can describe an earthquake as sudden ground shaking and say it can be strong or weak; they are NOT yet expected to explain the underground cause. Confront the 'giant crack swallows everything' myth and the idea that only objects (not the ground) move.
bestPractices: Simulate the felt experience (a scene that shakes) because a real earthquake can't be shown live — the concept is sensory
Make the WHOLE scene shake, floor included, so children grasp it is the ground moving, not just objects on it
Teach the strong–weak range explicitly with a simple intensity label ('barely felt' → 'very strong')
Tie to the body ('the floor wobbles like jelly') to make 'what it feels like' concrete and meet the evidence
Confront the 'ground opens and swallows people' myth directly with reassurance that shaking settles
Defer the underground cause (rocks breaking, energy released) to the 7–9 'Why Earthquakes Happen' topic
keyRepresentations: A shaking room scene with a strength dial (gentle → strong)
An intensity scale in words/faces ('barely felt' to 'very strong')
Everyday objects as shake-indicators (swinging lamp, rattling cup, sliding books)
A whole-scene wobble (including the floor/ground) to show the ground itself moves
commonMisconceptions: 'The ground opens up and swallows people/cars' — the ground shakes and settles; wide swallowing fissures are a movie myth
'Only the objects shake, not the ground' — it is the ground itself moving, which is why everything on it shakes
'An earthquake is an explosion/bomb underground' — it is shaking caused by rock movement (cause taught later), not a blast
'All earthquakes are huge and destructive' — most are weak; strength ranges from barely noticeable to very strong
'Earthquakes only happen far away / to other people' — they occur in many places, some regions much more than others

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach that an earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground that can be strong or weak. Secure two core ideas: (1) it is the GROUND ITSELF that shakes, not just the objects on it, and (2) earthquakes range in strength from barely felt to very strong. Keep the underground cause (rocks breaking and releasing energy) for the later 7–9 topic; here focus on WHAT an earthquake is and what it feels like. Directly confront the film myth that the ground 'opens up and swallows' people, reassuring that the shaking settles. The central activity lets children control a shaking scene so the felt, variable-intensity idea becomes experiential; supporting activities add naming, a recall check, and a reassuring personal account.

activities.title: Shake the room: feel strong and weak
feedback: When the floor shakes with everything else, point out: 'See how the ground moves, not just the cup — that is why everything wobbles at once.'
At the low setting: 'This is a weak earthquake — you might barely notice it. Real earthquakes can be this gentle.'
At the high setting: 'This is a strong one — things slide and tilt, but the ground shakes and then settles; it does not open up and swallow things.'
If a child expects the ground to split open, reassure: 'The ground shakes side to side and up and down, and may crack a little, but it does not open into a chasm that swallows people.'
activities.rationale: The target concept is a felt, dynamic intensity ('sudden shaking, strong or weak'), and a scene the child controls lets them experience the same event across the whole range under their own hand. Making the floor shake together with the objects makes 'it is the ground that moves' visible, and shows objects move because they rest on the moving ground. The strength dial, word/face readout, and body captions are optional supports that make the idea concrete. Because a real earthquake cannot be shown live, a controllable simulation is a reasonable stand-in; it may make the felt range more experiential than a still image, though this comparison is a design judgement rather than an established finding.
sourceClaims: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground; the ground rarely opens into a fissure that swallows people (a common myth)
learnerActions: Slide a strength dial from 'gentle' to 'strong' and watch the whole room respond
At the gentle end, notice a teacup and a hanging lamp just tremble
Nudge the dial higher and watch books slide, pictures tilt, and the shelf rattle
Notice that the FLOOR shakes too, along with everything else, so you can see it is the ground itself moving
Read the intensity label as it changes ('barely felt' → 'very strong') and say aloud what you would feel in your body at each setting
activities.intendedInsight: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground that can span from barely felt to very strong; because the ground itself moves, everything resting on it moves with it.

activities.title: Name what is happening in the shaking scene
feedback: 'The lamp swings because the ground under the whole room is moving.'
If a child says only the objects move: 'The shelf rattles because the ground it stands on is shaking — when the ground moves, everything resting on it moves with it.'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene can name visible effects and connect them to the underlying ground shaking. It is a useful naming and labelling support; a still or lightly animated scene conveys the strong/weak dimension less directly than a scene the child can actively intensify, so it works best alongside the controllable simulation.
learnerActions: Look at a scene of a shaking room and tap points such as the rattling shelf or swinging lamp
Read the one-line fact each tap reveals about what is happening
Say in your own words what an earthquake is doing to the room and to the ground
activities.intendedInsight: The signs of an earthquake (rattling, tilting, sliding) all happen because the ground is shaking.

activities.title: How strong, and what is an earthquake?
feedback: If the 'explosion' description is chosen: 'An earthquake is the ground shaking, not a blast or bomb. We will learn later what makes the ground shake.'
When the ordering is correct: 'Yes — from barely felt to very strong, earthquakes come in many strengths, and most are weak.'
activities.rationale: Short checks help confirm the definition and the weak→strong ordering. Recognition and ordering confirm recall but do not themselves deliver the felt experience of variable shaking, so use this after children have experienced the shaking rather than as a first encounter.
learnerActions: Read a described scene and set a strength slider to show how strong that earthquake was
Say what an earthquake is and choose the best description, rejecting an 'explosion underground' description
Put three earthquakes in order from weakest to strongest
activities.intendedInsight: An earthquake is ground shaking (not an explosion), and earthquakes can be ordered from weak to strong.

activities.title: Someone who felt an earthquake
feedback: 'The ground felt like it was wobbling like jelly, and then it stopped — the shaking does not go on forever; it settles.'
If a child seems worried: 'The shaking does not last forever, and the ground does not open up and swallow people.'
activities.rationale: A personal account can add vividness and reassurance and tie the concept to body experience. It works best as an optional add-on to the hands-on shaking activity rather than the main route to the concept for this age.
learnerActions: Listen to a friendly character describe feeling a small earthquake
Ask or choose questions like 'Was it scary?' and 'What did you do?'
Talk about what you would feel and do if the ground wobbled like jelly under your feet
activities.intendedInsight: An earthquake is something people feel in their bodies; a weak one can be barely noticeable, and the shaking settles.

constraints: Teach only WHAT an earthquake is and what it feels like at this age; defer the underground cause (rocks breaking, energy released) to the later 7–9 'Why Earthquakes Happen' topic.

Earthquakes are a KS2 Geography topic in England, and in the US NGSS K–2 standards they appear only as an example (the grade 2 standard 2-ESS1-1 gives earthquakes as an Earth event that happens quickly), so treat this as enrichment supported by observing and describing.

Directly address the 'ground opens and swallows people/cars' film myth with reassurance that the shaking settles; the ground shakes and may crack a little but does not form chasms that swallow people.

Make the whole scene (floor included) shake so children grasp that the ground itself moves, not just objects on it; objects move because the ground under them moves, though some (like sliding books or a swinging lamp) slide, tip or swing rather than moving exactly together with the floor.
The controllable simulation is a stand-in because a real earthquake cannot be shown live; it represents the felt experience rather than being an actual earthquake.
Recognition and ordering checks confirm recall but do not by themselves give the felt experience of variable shaking; use them after hands-on experience, not instead of it.

Interaction examples (strength dial, word/face intensity readout, tap-to-reveal points, swinging lamp, rattling cup, sliding books) are illustrative ways to make the idea concrete, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent editorial review: the prior correction of the activity-2 causal framing to simultaneity is sound, and no categorical medium-superiority claims remain; the remaining uncertainties are evidence-level, not learner-facing errors.
Source row marks the NGSS 2-ESS1-1 claim as verified; the DfE KS2 Geography placement claim and the USGS earthquake-basics/myth claim are marked unverified in the original.
The original stated a static picture 'cannot' convey shaking and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts, and have been softened to narrowly scoped trade-offs.
The 'earthquakes only happen far away / to other people' misconception from the source is not addressed in these activities and is left for a future extension.
'Most earthquakes are weak' is retained from the source; confirm it fits the local/regional context when used.

probeDeeper: If an earthquake was very weak, what might it feel like — could you even notice it?
Does the ground stay open after an earthquake, or does the shaking just stop?
What would you feel in your body if you were standing up during a strong earthquake?
Is a tiny trembling of the ground still an earthquake, or does it have to be huge to count?
assess.correctAnswer: No — that's a film exaggeration. In a real earthquake the ground shakes suddenly, side to side and up and down; it doesn't split open into a chasm that swallows people. The shaking can be so weak you barely notice it, or strong enough to be frightening.

errorPatterns.pattern: The ground opens into a huge crack and swallows people and cars
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the film myth — the ground shakes and may crack a little, but big openings that swallow people don't happen; reassure them.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the ground opens up and swallows people.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a chasm that people fall into and disappear.

errorPatterns.pattern: Every earthquake is huge and knocks everything down (doesn't know they vary in strength)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Most earthquakes are so weak we don't even feel them; introduce a strength range from barely-felt to very strong.
errorPatterns.distractor: An earthquake always shakes so hard it knocks buildings down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes all earthquakes are catastrophic; no idea that most are weak.

responseLevels.gap: Believes the ground opens and swallows people; equates an earthquake with a chasm.
responseLevels.full: Describes an earthquake as sudden ground shaking that ranges from barely-felt to very strong, rejects the swallowing/chasm myth, and can say what the shaking would feel like.
responseLevels.partial: Says an earthquake is the ground shaking but still thinks it always opens the ground or is always huge.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a film, the ground rips open into a giant crack during an earthquake and people fall in. Does that really happen in an earthquake? What does an earthquake actually do to the ground?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can define an earthquake as 'the ground shaking' (first tier) yet still believe the ground opens and swallows people. Asking what actually happens to the ground forces 'shaking, not a chasm' — a child holding the myth describes the ground opening up and people falling in.
